## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- codebase-memory: Use the codebase knowledge graph for structural code queries. Triggers on: explore the codebase, understand the architecture, what functions exist, show me the structure, who calls this function, what does X call, trace the call chain, find callers of, show dependencies, impact analysis, dead code, unused functions, high fan-out, refactor candidates, code quality audit, graph query syntax, Cypher query examples, edge types, how to use search_graph.
- commit: Commit pending changes split into logical change sets, each with a Conventional Commits message prefixed by a relevant emoji. Use when the user asks to commit, group/stage changes into logical commits, or write conventional-commit messages with emoji (gitmoji-style).
- development-docs: Decide whether anything from the current session belongs in docs/DEVELOPMENT.md (recurring dev patterns) or docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md (bugs/gotchas), and record it with a cited source if so. Use before finalizing a commit (invoked as a step of the commit skill, and reminded by a pre-commit hook), or when the user explicitly asks to record a pattern, gotcha, or lesson learned.
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- council:council: Convene the Council of High Intelligence — multi-persona deliberation with historical thinkers for deeper analysis of complex problems.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	export const meta = {
2	  name: 'refactor-long-functions',
3	  description: 'Find functions >100 lines, propose refactors per file, independently verify each, dedupe, report',
4	  phases: [
5	    { title: 'Analyze' },
6	    { title: 'Dedupe' },
7	    { title: 'Verify' },
8	  ],
9	}
10	
11	const FILES = args.files
12	
13	const ANALYZE_SCHEMA = {
14	  type: 'object',
15	  properties: {
16	    file: { type: 'string' },
17	    functions: {
18	      type: 'array',
19	      items: {
20	        type: 'object',
21	        properties: {
22	          name: { type: 'string' },
23	          start_line: { type: 'number' },
24	          end_line: { type: 'number' },
25	          length: { type: 'number' },
26	          refactor_proposal: { type: 'string' },
27	          rationale: { type: 'string' },
28	        },
29	        required: ['name', 'start_line', 'end_line', 'length', 'refactor_proposal', 'rationale'],
30	      },
31	    },
32	  },
33	  required: ['file', 'functions'],
34	}
35	
36	const VERIFY_SCHEMA = {
37	  type: 'object',
38	  properties: {
39	    verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['approve', 'revise', 'reject'] },
40	    comments: { type: 'string' },
41	  },
42	  required: ['verdict', 'comments'],
43	}
44	
45	phase('Analyze')
46	const analyzeResults = await parallel(FILES.map(f => () =>
47	  agent(
48	    `Read the Python file ${f.path} in the wakil repo (a local-first Markdown knowledge-base CLI agent; keep proposals boring, local, simple — no speculative abstractions, no new frameworks, per project engineering principle). ` +
49	    `The following functions in this file are known to exceed 100 lines: ${JSON.stringify(f.functions)}. ` +
50	    `For EACH of these functions, read its full body at the given line range and propose a concrete refactor to bring it under 100 lines (e.g. extract helper functions, split responsibilities, remove duplication). ` +
51	    `Do not propose introducing new abstractions or frameworks beyond what's needed to shrink the function. ` +
52	    `Return one entry per function with a specific refactor_proposal (what to extract/split, named helpers) and a short rationale.`,
53	    { label: `analyze:${f.path}`, phase: 'Analyze', schema: ANALYZE_SCHEMA }
54	  ).then(r => ({ ...r, __requested: f.path })).catch(() => null)
55	))
56	
57	log(`Analyze phase: ${analyzeResults.filter(Boolean).length}/${FILES.length} files returned proposals`)
58	
59	phase('Dedupe')
60	const seen = new Set()
61	const proposals = []
62	for (const r of analyzeResults) {
63	  if (!r) continue
64	  for (const fn of (r.functions || [])) {
65	    const key = `${r.file}::${fn.name}::${fn.start_line}`
66	    if (seen.has(key)) continue
67	    seen.add(key)
68	    proposals.push({ file: r.file, ...fn })
69	  }
70	}
71	log(`Dedupe phase: ${proposals.length} unique proposals after dedup (from ${analyzeResults.filter(Boolean).reduce((n, r) => n + (r.functions?.length || 0), 0)} raw)`)
72	
73	phase('Verify')
74	const verified = await parallel(proposals.map(p => () =>
75	  agent(
76	    `You are an independent reviewer with no prior context on this task. In the wakil repo (a local-first Markdown knowledge-base CLI agent that values simple, boring, explicit code over speculative abstraction), someone proposed this refactor:\n\n` +
77	    `File: ${p.file}\nFunction: ${p.name} (lines ${p.start_line}-${p.end_line}, ${p.length} lines)\nProposal: ${p.refactor_proposal}\nRationale: ${p.rationale}\n\n` +
78	    `Read the actual function in the file at that line range and judge the proposal on its merits: is it correct (does it actually reduce length / improve clarity), is it safe (preserves behavior), and is it proportionate (no unneeded abstraction per the project's anti-over-engineering principle)? ` +
79	    `Return a verdict of approve, revise, or reject, with specific comments.`,
80	    { label: `verify:${p.file}:${p.name}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERIFY_SCHEMA }
81	  ).then(v => ({ ...p, verdict: v })).catch(() => ({ ...p, verdict: null }))
82	))
83	
84	const missingVerify = verified.filter(v => !v.verdict).length
85	if (missingVerify > 0) log(`WARNING: ${missingVerify} proposals failed verification and have no verdict`)
86	
87	return {
88	  files_scanned: FILES.length,
89	  files_with_proposals: analyzeResults.filter(Boolean).length,
90	  files_failed: FILES.length - analyzeResults.filter(Boolean).length,
91	  raw_proposal_count: analyzeResults.filter(Boolean).reduce((n, r) => n + (r.functions?.length || 0), 0),
92	  deduped_proposal_count: proposals.length,
93	  verified,
94	}

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

input.description: Refactor validate_proposal in ingest_service.py
input.prompt:
Repo: wakil (local-first Python CLI for a Markdown knowledge base). You're working in an isolated git worktree — make commits freely, don't push anywhere.

Task: refactor `validate_proposal` in `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py` (currently lines ~2027-2129, 103 lines) to bring it under 100 lines. A prior review round already designed and verified this refactor, in two parts — one approved as-is, one that needs a correction from what was originally drafted:

**Part A (approved as-is): split into three validation-pass functions.** The function runs three independent validation passes over three different collections (`proposed_files`, `entity_updates`, `entity_resolutions`), each appending to one shared `issues` list, with no data dependency between passes and no test anywhere asserting cross-pass issue ordering. Extract:
- `_validate_proposed_files(proposed_files, schemas, kb_root) -> list[ProposalIssue]` — the path-dup check, frontmatter/schema validation, and directory-placement check (roughly lines 2053-2087).
- `_validate_entity_updates(entity_updates, kb_root) -> list[ProposalIssue]` — roughly lines 2091-2106.
- `_validate_unroutable_creates(entity_resolutions, schemas) -> list[ProposalIssue]` — roughly lines 2109-2128.

`validate_proposal` itself becomes: build `proposed_files` (proposed_note + stub_entities), load `schemas`, then `issues = [*_validate_proposed_files(...), *_validate_entity_updates(...), *_validate_unroutable_creates(...)]`, return `issues`.

**Part B (needs correction — do NOT implement the naive version): do not add one shared frontmatter-type parser across the first two loops.** An earlier draft proposed extracting a single `_parse_entity_type(content) -> tuple[str | None, dict]` used by both the proposed_files loop and the entity_updates loop, returning `(None, {})` uniformly on either a parse exception or a missing `type:` field. This is WRONG and must not be implemented that way, because the two loops currently handle a parse exception differently and this matters for users:
- The proposed_files loop, on a frontmatter parse exception, swallows it (`metadata = {}`) and falls through to the type check, which reports the generic "proposed file has no `type:` frontmatter" issue.
- The entity_updates loop, on a parse exception, appends a distinct, more specific issue — "merged content is not valid frontmatter" — and `continue`s immediately, without ever reaching the type-check line.
Collapsing these into one shared parser that returns `(None, {})` for both cases would make `_validate_entity_updates` unable to distinguish "genuinely broken YAML from a merge" from "valid frontmatter but missing `type:`" — silently downgrading a real corruption signal to a generic schema complaint. (No existing test would catch this regression — the only entity_updates test that touches frontmatter validity, `test_validate_proposal_rejects_entity_update_with_invalid_frontmatter`, exercises a bad enum value, not a YAML parse failure — so get this right on the first pass rather than relying on the test suite to catch it.)

Instead, only extract what's genuinely identical between the two loops — just the narrow metadata-to-entity_type step:
```python
entity_type = metadata.get("type") if isinstance(metadata, dict) else None
if not isinstance(entity_type, str) or not entity_type:
    ...
```
e.g. as a small `_entity_type_of(metadata: dict) -> str | None` helper — and leave each loop's own `frontmatter_lib.loads(...)` call and its own `try/except` (with its own distinct error message) in place, unchanged, inside `_validate_proposed_files` and `_validate_entity_updates` respectively.

Project conventions to respect (this repo's CLAUDE.md, which you should read at the repo root): keep changes small, no speculative abstractions, no new classes/frameworks, boring explicit Python. This is a pure refactor — the only behavioral requirement is that both distinct parse-exception messages must still be produced exactly as they are today.

Confirm they all pass, and specifically confirm `test_validate_proposal_rejects_entity_update_with_invalid_frontmatter` (or equivalent) still gets the distinct entity_updates error message, not the generic proposed_files one.

input.prompt:

Task: refactor `traverse` in `src/wakil/app/graph_service.py` (currently lines ~62-211, 150 lines) to bring it under 100 lines. A prior review round already designed and verified this refactor, with a correction to the original draft's split.

The original draft proposed 5 helpers, splitting SQL construction into two separate functions. That was pushed back on: this module's own docstring commits to "a single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE" as the deliberate design, and the inline comments explain the seed/step/aggregation logic as one contiguous story. Splitting the SQL construction into two functions would force a reader auditing the hand-written SQL (the part most worth auditing carefully) to jump between two functions instead of reading one block top to bottom — a real clarity cost. The claimed testability benefit of splitting it two ways is also weak: a unit test of SQL-building code in isolation can only assert exact string/TextClause equality, not that the CTE actually walks the graph correctly; the behavior that matters (depth clamping, cycle termination, direction merge/dedup, predicate filtering, missing-anchor errors) is already covered end-to-end against a live session by the 14 existing tests in `tests/unit/test_graph_service.py`.

Implement it with 4 helpers instead of 5 — keep the SQL construction as ONE merged function, not two, so the seed/step fragments and the outer WITH RECURSIVE template stay adjacent and readable as a single unit:

1. `_validate_and_clamp_depth(depth: int, direction: str) -> int` — the argument validation plus the MAX_TRAVERSAL_DEPTH clamp (roughly lines 77-83). Returns the clamped depth or raises `TraversalError`.
2. `_resolve_anchor(session, workspace_id, anchor_path) -> tuple[int, str | None]` — the anchor SELECT plus not-found check (roughly lines 85-91). Raises `TraversalError` on a missing note.
3. `_build_traversal_sql(direction) -> TextClause` (a single merged function — do NOT split this into two) — combines what would have been the seed/step SQL fragment assembly (roughly lines 93-143) AND the WITH RECURSIVE / best_depth / outer SELECT template plus `.bindparams(...)` (roughly lines 145-181) into one function keyed off `direction`, returning the fully-built `TextClause`. Keep the seed/step fragments referencing bind placeholders (`:ws`/`:anchor_id`/`:predicate`) exactly as they do today — verify there's no hidden coupling requiring literal Python values instead of bind params.
4. `_hits_from_rows(rows) -> list[TraversalHit]` — the row-to-dataclass mapping (roughly lines 193-203).

After extraction, `traverse()` itself should read as: validate/clamp depth, resolve anchor, build the query via `_build_traversal_sql`, execute it, map rows to hits via `_hits_from_rows`, construct and return `TraversalResult` — no behavior change, no new classes, no config objects, same single-CTE strategy the module docstring commits to.

## PR #108 Review — extract oversized-compiled-truth menu loop from `entities_compile`

**Verified independently** (checked out `pr-108`, did not just trust the description):
- `uv run ruff check .` → All checks passed.
- `uv run pytest -q -m "not eval"` → 621 passed, 62 deselected — matches the PR description's numbers exactly.
- Read ADR 0017 in full (the ADR this menu implements) and `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` / `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md` (both have prior entries about this exact edit-flow's hang bug, but nothing that conflicts with this PR). README has no `entities compile` section, so no doc update was owed here — this is a pure internal refactor with no user-visible behavior change.

### Correctness of the extraction — confirmed correct

The core claim (bare `return` inside the new helper would only unwind the helper, not the whole `entities_compile` command, so the `f` branch needed `raise typer.Exit(code=0)` instead) is right, and I traced it line-by-line against the pre-PR code in `src/wakil/cli/main.py`:

- Old: `f` branch did `_run_full_resynthesis(); return` — a bare `return` from inside `entities_compile`'s own body exits the whole command function.
- New: the loop lives in module-level `_resolve_oversized_compiled_truth`; a bare `return` there would only return control to the call site inside `entities_compile`, which would then fall through to `print_entity_update_preview(update)` / a second `typer.confirm` / `_apply_and_commit(update, "compile")` using the *stale, pre-loop* `update` — re-previewing and potentially re-applying over a file that full resynthesis already wrote and (optionally) committed. `raise typer.Exit(code=0)` correctly propagates past all of that since it's an exception, not a return value, and nothing in `entities_compile` catches bare `typer.Exit`.
- This is exercised by an existing test that would have caught a regression here: `tests/integration/test_ingest_cli.py::test_entities_compile_over_target_menu_full_resynthesis` (`src/wakil/cli/main.py` PR / `tests/integration/test_ingest_cli.py:649-667`) drives `input="f\ny\n"` with exactly two scripted model responses. If the bare-return bug were present, execution would fall through to a third, unscripted `typer.confirm` call with no remaining stdin — the test would fail (EOF/abort) rather than pass. I confirmed this test is in the 621 passing.
- The `c` (cancel) branch was already `raise typer.Exit(code=0)` before the refactor (it never relied on bare `return`), so it needed no change — the PR correctly left it alone rather than "fixing" something that wasn't broken.
- The `a` branch and the successful-edit-under-target case both `return update` from the helper, which correctly mirrors the old code's `break` (fall through to the same post-loop preview/confirm/apply tail). Traced this too; no divergence.

I did not find a behavior discrepancy between old and new code paths.

### Fit with CLAUDE.md / repo conventions

- Proportionate: this is a straight extraction (182 → ~117 lines in `entities_compile`), no new CLI flag, no new config knob, no new abstraction layer — squarely within "keep changes small," not scope creep.
- No ADR is reopened or contradicted. It doesn't touch ingestion dispatch (ADR 0008), doesn't add a new write path around git (ADR 0003), doesn't add a parallel DB copy of note content (ADR 0007). It's a refactor of ADR 0017's already-accepted interactive menu, not a redesign of it.
- Deliberately leaves `_apply_and_commit`/`_run_full_resynthesis` as closures inside `entities_compile` (they close over `slug`, `commit`, `yes`, `config`, `client`) while making `_resolve_oversized_compiled_truth` a top-level function taking its dependencies as explicit parameters (`update`, `text`, `size`, `run_full_resynthesis` passed in). That's a reasonable, minimal-surface choice — it only extracts the piece that doesn't need the wider closure state, and it's the piece complex enough (nested menu/edit/retry logic) to benefit from being independently readable.
- Local-import style (`import click`, `from wakil.app.ingest_service import ...` inside the function body) matches this file's existing convention throughout (`main.py` does this in every other command function too) — not a new pattern.

### Minor / non-blocking

1. **Untyped callable parameter.** `src/wakil/cli/main.py` — `_resolve_oversized_compiled_truth(..., *, run_full_resynthesis)` has no type annotation on `run_full_resynthesis`. This repo already has the right idiom for exactly this (`ingest_service.py:2565`, `speaker_of: Callable[[dict], str]`). Since there's no type checker running in CI to catch this, it's worth typing as `Callable[[], None]` at review time rather than letting a second untyped-callable convention start alongside the existing typed one.
2. **No new direct unit test for the extracted helper.** `_resolve_oversized_compiled_truth` is now an independently-callable, independently-testable function, but coverage still comes entirely through the existing CLI-level integration tests (`tests/integration/test_ingest_cli.py`, the `test_entities_compile_over_target_*` family) exercising it through the full Typer command. That existing coverage is genuinely thorough — I checked it covers all seven branches (apply-as-is, cancel, empty edit, timeline-heading collision, cancelled edit, still-over-target edit, successful edit, full-resynthesis) — so this is a nice-to-have for future edits to this function, not a gap in this PR.
3. Minor duplication: `_COMPILED_TRUTH_TARGET_CHARS` is now imported locally in both `entities_compile` and the new helper. Harmless and consistent with this file's per-function lazy-import convention; noting only for completeness, not a request for change.

### Bottom line

The extraction is correct, the specific bug it names and fixes (return-vs-Exit) is real and would otherwise have been introduced by this refactor, and it's backed by a test that actually exercises the failure mode rather than just asserting on the happy path. Ruff and the non-eval test suite pass as claimed when run independently. Scope is proportionate to CLAUDE.md's anti-over-engineering stance — no new abstraction, no new user-facing surface. The only asks are a one-line type annotation and an optional future unit test; neither blocks merging.

# Agent guidance

## Project

This repository contains `wakil`, a local-first Python CLI agent for working with a personal Markdown knowledge base.

`wakil` is designed for one user working locally on knowledge work, not coding automation. The target knowledge base is GBrain / Obsidian style: Markdown files, links, concepts, notes, meeting transcripts, web clippings, source material, journal entries, and synthesis documents.

The goal is to help the user ingest, search, connect, revise, and reason over a Markdown knowledge base.

The project thesis is:

> Build a local, git-native knowledge-work agent that helps a single user discover useful connections, maintain a Markdown knowledge base, and turn raw inputs into durable, searchable memory.

The engineering principle is:

> Keep the implementation simple unless added complexity has a clear and self-evident impact on the target use case.

Do not over-engineer this project.

---

## Python Stack

Use modern Python and boring local infrastructure.

```text id="olf5zd"
Python 3.12+
uv
Pydantic v2
Typer
Rich / Textual-friendly output patterns
SQLite
SQLAlchemy
Alembic
httpx
BeautifulSoup / readability-lxml for article extraction
python-frontmatter
markdown-it-py
PyYAML
GitPython or subprocess git wrapper
pytest
ruff
ty
```

Model access should be provider-abstracted but minimal:

```text id="p1muyf"
OpenAI-compatible endpoint
Anthropic
Gemini or other provider later only if needed
local model endpoint later if useful
```

Search:

```text id="lch4np"
QMD as first-class search
SQLite FTS5 for internal records
optional embeddings later
optional Neo4J deep dive later
```

---

## Prime Directive

Build the smallest useful version of `wakil` that advances the local knowledge-work use case.

Before adding abstraction, ask:

```question
Does this clearly improve local Markdown knowledge work for one user?
```

If the answer is not obviously yes, do not add it.

Prefer simple, explicit, boring Python code over clever frameworks or speculative architecture.

---

## Design Biases

Prefer:

```text
simple local workflows
Markdown as source of truth
SQLite as operational store
QMD as first-class search
git-native changes
clear memory lifecycle
human review
rich CLI output
grounded citations
explicit commands
small composable services
```

Avoid:

```text
remote runtimes
complex permissions
large agent frameworks
hidden background behavior
automatic rewriting without review
multi-agent orchestration
premature graph databases
opaque memory systems
overly abstract plugin architectures
hosted product assumptions
```

---

## Working Agreement for Agents

When contributing to this repo:

1. Keep changes small.
2. Do not add speculative abstractions.
3. Preserve the local-first CLI focus.
4. Prefer Markdown, SQLite, QMD, and Git over new infrastructure.
5. Avoid building for multi-user or hosted deployment yet.
6. Keep model behavior behind deterministic application controls.
7. Add tests for meaningful behavior.
8. Update docs when behavior changes.
9. Respect the distinction between raw sources, durable notes, and memory.
10. Treat sensitive content carefully.
11. Show reviewable diffs for knowledge-base modifications — a pre-write
    preview for direct CLI/tool use, or the resulting pull request for an
    agent following the `mcp-coordinator` skill over MCP (docs/adr/0019).
    Both satisfy this item; it does not mean every write must block on a
    human immediately before it happens, in every context.
12. Do not silently rewrite user knowledge.

The project should feel like a careful local knowledge assistant, not a sprawling agent platform.

        f"# {name}\n\n"

# The Compiled Truth / Open Threads span _stub_content writes at creation
# time, independent of entity name or frontmatter (both live outside this
# span) — derived from _stub_content itself rather than duplicated as a
# second literal, so the two can never silently drift apart. Used to detect
# an entity that has NEVER been populated, so a declined update against it
# can be flagged with a much higher-severity warning than "this particular
# update was skipped" (issue #45).
_stub_sections = _split_note_sections(frontmatter_lib.loads(_stub_content({}, "_")).content)
assert _stub_sections is not None
_STUB_TOP_SECTION = _stub_sections[1]
del _stub_sections


def _is_unpopulated_stub(content: str) -> bool:
    """True if `content` (a full note file, frontmatter included) still has
    exactly the Compiled Truth placeholder `_stub_content` writes at
    creation time — i.e. nothing has ever synthesized real content into it,
    across however many enrich passes have touched the entity since."""
    try:
        post = frontmatter_lib.loads(content)
    except Exception:
        return False
    sections = _split_note_sections(post.content)
    if sections is None:
        return False
    _, top_section, _ = sections
    return top_section.strip() == _STUB_TOP_SECTION


def validate_proposal(
    proposal: EnrichmentProposal, kb_root: Path | None = None
) -> list[ProposalIssue]:
    """Invariant gate between prepare and apply; any issue blocks the write.

    Implements entity-resolution.md's constraints plus the schema check:
    every proposed new file must carry frontmatter valid against its entity
    schema; a pending create for a type with no schema at all is a hard
    stop, not a best-guess write (types that have a schema but no canonical
    directory, e.g. `index`, are instead warned about and dropped from
    proposal.entity_resolutions upstream in _build_stub_entities, so this
    loop never sees them); no two proposed files may share a path. Routing
    is 1:N by construction (proposed_note + stub_entities), and content-hash
    dedup is already enforced upstream at capture time.

    `kb_root` should be the workspace root so a kb-local schema override
    validates against the same schema extraction/entity-resolution used —
    omitted only by tests that don't exercise the override mechanism.
    """
    issues: list[ProposalIssue] = []
    schemas = load_entity_schemas(kb_root)

    proposed_files = list(proposal.stub_entities)
    if proposal.proposed_note is not None:
        proposed_files.insert(0, proposal.proposed_note)

    seen_paths: set[str] = set()
    for proposed in proposed_files:
        if proposed.path in seen_paths:
            issues.append(ProposalIssue(proposed.path, "duplicate proposed path"))
        seen_paths.add(proposed.path)
        try:
            metadata = frontmatter_lib.loads(proposed.content).metadata
        except Exception:
            metadata = {}
        entity_type = metadata.get("type") if isinstance(metadata, dict) else None
        if not isinstance(entity_type, str) or not entity_type:
            issues.append(ProposalIssue(proposed.path, "proposed file has no `type:` frontmatter"))
            continue
        for error in validate_frontmatter(entity_type, metadata, kb_root):
            issues.append(ProposalIssue(proposed.path, str(error)))

        # Placement: a new page's directory must sit under its own type's
        # schema.directory (a subdirectory is fine, e.g. "meetings/2026/...")
        # — `_build_stub_entities` already routes stubs this way by
        # construction; the model-chosen primary note gets no such
        # guarantee, so it's checked here instead. A real routing bug, not
        # cosmetic drift, so this is a hard stop rather than an
        # auto-correction — unlike a filename/H1 slug mismatch.
        schema = schemas.get(entity_type)
        if schema is not None and schema.directory is not None:
            schema_dir = schema.directory.rstrip("/")
            proposed_dir = Path(proposed.path).parent.as_posix()
            if proposed_dir != schema_dir and not proposed_dir.startswith(f"{schema_dir}/"):
                issues.append(
                    ProposalIssue(
                        proposed.path,
                        f"type '{entity_type}' pages belong under {schema_dir}/, "
                        f"not {proposed_dir}/",
                    )
                )

    # Edits to existing notes must still satisfy their type's schema —
    # frontmatter_updates could otherwise merge in a value that breaks it.
    for update in proposal.entity_updates:
        try:
            metadata = frontmatter_lib.loads(update.new_content).metadata
        except Exception:
            issues.append(
                ProposalIssue(update.target_note_path, "merged content is not valid frontmatter")
            )
            continue
        entity_type = metadata.get("type") if isinstance(metadata, dict) else None
        if not isinstance(entity_type, str) or not entity_type:
            issues.append(
                ProposalIssue(update.target_note_path, "merged file has no `type:` frontmatter")
            )
            continue
        for error in validate_frontmatter(entity_type, metadata, kb_root):
            issues.append(ProposalIssue(update.target_note_path, str(error)))

    # Creates that could not even build a stub: missing schema or directory.
    for resolution in proposal.entity_resolutions:
        if resolution.action != "create":
            continue
        schema = schemas.get(resolution.entity_type)
        if schema is None:
            issues.append(
                ProposalIssue(
                    f"entity:{resolution.name}",
                    f"no entity schema defines type '{resolution.entity_type}' "
                    f"(known: {', '.join(sorted(schemas))})",
                )
            )
        elif schema.directory is None:
            issues.append(
                ProposalIssue(
                    f"entity:{resolution.name}",
                    f"type '{resolution.entity_type}' has no canonical directory to "
                    "route a new page into",
                )
            )
    return issues


def _write_new_proposed_files(config: WorkspaceConfig, proposal: EnrichmentProposal) -> list[str]:
    files_written: list[str] = []
    proposed_files = list(proposal.stub_entities)
    if proposal.proposed_note is not None:
        proposed_files.insert(0, proposal.proposed_note)
    for proposed in proposed_files:
        target = config.root_path / proposed.path

### Adding a mandatory model call to the enrichment DAG means auditing every `FakeClient(...)` construction, not just bumping a default
**Established:** 2026-07-27 · **Source:** issue #70, `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`'s `_synthesize_stub_content`, `tests/unit/test_ingest_service.py`

`prepare_enrichment`'s DAG (extraction → entity-resolution → entity-updates → …) is exercised almost entirely through `FakeClient`, a fixed-length scripted-response queue with no notion of "this call is optional" — each test's list length has to exactly match however many real model calls that specific resolution shape triggers. Adding a new *unconditional* call partway through the DAG (here: synthesize content for every create-resolution's stub once it survives suppression) broke every test whose fixture happened to produce that condition, not just the ones that explicitly asserted a call count — including tests using the bare default `FakeClient()` and tests with an explicit 2-3-item list built for the DAG shape *before* the new call existed. There is no shortcut around this: bumping `FakeClient.__init__`'s default queue only covers bare `FakeClient()` callers; every explicit-list construction still has to be individually re-derived (does this resolution's create survive suppression? does an update-candidate's target file exist on disk?) and given one more scripted response, or the test fails opaquely with "FakeClient ran out of scripted responses" rather than a clear diff. When adding a new call to this (or any other) fixed-length-fake-backed DAG, budget time to grep every construction site of the fake client, not just its default, before trusting a green test run.

### MCP tools live in `mcp/tools.py` as plain functions; `mcp/server.py` wraps them in closures for FastMCP registration
**Established:** 2026-07-28 · **Source:** `docs/adr/0018-mcp-interface.md`, `src/wakil/mcp/tools.py`/`server.py`

FastMCP's `@mcp.tool()` decorator introspects the wrapped function's signature to build the tool's client-facing JSON schema — any parameter present on that function becomes something the MCP client is expected to supply. Every wakil MCP tool needs a `WorkspaceConfig` (and the write tools need the shared `ProposalCache`) that must stay fixed for the life of one `wakil mcp serve` process, not be re-supplied per call, so those can't be plain parameters on the decorated function. `mcp/tools.py` holds the actual logic as ordinary functions taking `config`/`cache` explicitly first, directly unit-testable with no running server (`tests/unit/test_mcp_tools.py` calls them with no MCP machinery at all); `mcp/server.py`'s `build_server(config)` builds one `ProposalCache`, then registers a thin closure per tool that captures `config`/`cache` and forwards only the remaining, client-facing parameters. The next new MCP tool should follow the same split — logic in `tools.py`, a same-named closure wrapper in `server.py` — rather than writing logic directly inside a `@mcp.tool()`-decorated function.

### Stacked same-file refactor PRs from a shared base conflict on sequential merge even when the functions they touch don't overlap
**Established:** 2026-07-30 · **Source:** PRs #109, #110, #111 (three independent function-level refactors of `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`, each branched from the same pre-refactor commit)

Three worktree-agent PRs each extracted helpers from a *different* function in `ingest_service.py` (`apply_enrichment`, `_build_stub_entities`, `validate_proposal`), with no line ranges in common. Merging the first two into `main` sequentially was a clean fast-forward, but the third (`validate_proposal`) then failed `gh pr merge` with a conflict, because git's diff anchors on the *text* around a change, not on which named function it belongs to — once `apply_enrichment`'s body was replaced by a call to its new helpers on `main`, the region immediately following the still-unrefactored (from that branch's point of view) `validate_proposal` no longer matched what the `validate_proposal` branch expected to find there, even though neither PR touched the other's actual function body. Rebasing the trailing branch onto the new `main` reproduces the same conflict (it's not merge-order-specific); resolving it requires re-deriving the intended final file — start from `main`'s current version of the file and manually re-apply just the extracted-function's diff, rather than trying to hand-resolve `<<<<<<<`/`>>>>>>>` markers in place, since the marked regions don't line up with either branch's actual intended change. When queuing multiple same-file refactor PRs from one audit, expect this on any PR after the first that touches that file, and budget for a manual reconciliation pass rather than a routine merge.

Implement:

Split `build_server` into four small module-level registration helpers, each taking the already-constructed `mcp` (and `config`/`cache` as needed) and registering one cohesive group of tools/resources via the same `@mcp.tool()`/`@mcp.resource()` decorators already in use — no new registration mechanism, just grouping by responsibility:
1. `_register_coordinator_resource(mcp: FastMCP) -> None` — the `wakil://skill/mcp-coordinator` resource and its `mcp_coordinator_skill()` reader.
2. `_register_read_tools(mcp: FastMCP, config: WorkspaceConfig) -> None` — the read-only knowledge-base tools: status, search, query, memory_list, memory_show, relationships, sources_list, sources_show, skills_list.
3. `_register_git_tools(mcp: FastMCP, config: WorkspaceConfig) -> None` — git_summary and git_history.
4. `_register_write_tools(mcp: FastMCP, config: WorkspaceConfig, cache: ProposalCache) -> None` — the prepare/apply pairs: ingest_prepare, ingest_apply, enrich_prepare, enrich_apply.

`build_server` then shrinks to constructing `mcp = FastMCP("wakil")` and `cache = ProposalCache()`, calling the four helpers with `mcp`/`config`/`cache`, and returning `mcp`.

REQUIRED CORRECTION (an earlier draft's line-range citations for this split were wrong and would mis-group tools if followed literally — do not copy them): the tools are NOT laid out in the file in the tidy "read tools, then git tools, then skills_list" order you might assume. In the actual file, the git tools (git_summary/git_history) physically sit *inside* the middle of what should be the "read tools" range, and skills_list comes physically after the git tools despite being a read tool. Read the actual file and group by which named tool function you're moving (status, search, query, memory_list, memory_show, relationships, sources_list, sources_show, skills_list → read tools; git_summary, git_history → git tools; ingest_prepare, ingest_apply, enrich_prepare, enrich_apply → write tools; the one `wakil://skill/mcp-coordinator` resource → its own group), not by copying any pre-existing line-range assumption. Python doesn't care about physical order, so pulling `skills_list` and the two git tools out from wherever they actually sit in the file into their correct logical groups is fine and expected.

def _resolve_context_or_exit(
    context: list[str] | None, context_file: list[Path] | None, workspace_root: Path
) -> "ResolvedContext | None":
    from wakil.app.context_references import ContextResolutionError, resolve_context

    try:
        resolved, warnings = resolve_context(
            context=context or [],
            context_files=context_file or [],
            workspace_root=workspace_root,
        )
    except ContextResolutionError as exc:
        console.print(f"[red]Context resolution failed:[/red] {exc}")
        raise typer.Exit(code=1) from exc
    for warning in warnings:
        console.print(f"[yellow]Warning:[/yellow] {warning}")
    return resolved


def _prepare_enrichment_or_exit(
    config: WorkspaceConfig,
    *,
    source_id: int,
    client,
    resolved_context: "ResolvedContext | None",
    force: bool,
    landing,
):
    from wakil.app.git_service import abandon_landing
    from wakil.app.ingest_service import IngestError, prepare_enrichment
    from wakil.llm.client import ModelError

    try:
        with console.status(f"Analyzing source #{source_id} with {client.model}..."):
            return prepare_enrichment(
                config,
                source_id,
                client,
                context=resolved_context.text if resolved_context else None,
                context_digest=resolved_context.digest if resolved_context else None,
                context_referenced_paths=(
                    resolved_context.referenced_paths if resolved_context else None
                ),
                force=force,
            )
    except (IngestError, ModelError) as exc:
        console.print(f"[red]Enrichment failed:[/red] {exc}")
        abandon_landing(config, landing)
        raise typer.Exit(code=1) from exc


def _confirm_and_apply_enrichment(config: WorkspaceConfig, proposal, landing, yes: bool):
    from wakil.app.git_service import abandon_landing
    from wakil.app.ingest_service import IngestError, apply_enrichment, validate_proposal

    print_enrichment_proposal(proposal)
    issues = validate_proposal(proposal, kb_root=config.root_path)
    if issues:
        print_proposal_issues(issues)
        abandon_landing(config, landing)
        raise typer.Exit(code=1)
    if not yes and not typer.confirm("Apply this enrichment (write files, record memories)?"):
        console.print("Aborted; nothing was written.")
        abandon_landing(config, landing)
        raise typer.Exit(code=0)

    try:
        result = apply_enrichment(config, proposal)
    except IngestError as exc:
        console.print(f"[red]Enrichment failed:[/red] {exc}")
        abandon_landing(config, landing)
        raise typer.Exit(code=1) from exc
    print_enrichment_result(result)
    return result

# Agent guidance

## Project

This repository contains `wakil`, a local-first Python CLI agent for working with a personal Markdown knowledge base.

`wakil` is designed for one user working locally on knowledge work, not coding automation. The target knowledge base is GBrain / Obsidian style: Markdown files, links, concepts, notes, meeting transcripts, web clippings, source material, journal entries, and synthesis documents.

The goal is to help the user ingest, search, connect, revise, and reason over a Markdown knowledge base.

The project thesis is:

> Build a local, git-native knowledge-work agent that helps a single user discover useful connections, maintain a Markdown knowledge base, and turn raw inputs into durable, searchable memory.

The engineering principle is:

> Keep the implementation simple unless added complexity has a clear and self-evident impact on the target use case.

Do not over-engineer this project.

---

## Python Stack

Use modern Python and boring local infrastructure.

```text id="olf5zd"
Python 3.12+
uv
Pydantic v2
Typer
Rich / Textual-friendly output patterns
SQLite
SQLAlchemy
Alembic
httpx
BeautifulSoup / readability-lxml for article extraction
python-frontmatter
markdown-it-py
PyYAML
GitPython or subprocess git wrapper
pytest
ruff
ty
```

Model access should be provider-abstracted but minimal:

```text id="p1muyf"
OpenAI-compatible endpoint
Anthropic
Gemini or other provider later only if needed
local model endpoint later if useful
```

Search:

```text id="lch4np"
QMD as first-class search
SQLite FTS5 for internal records
optional embeddings later
optional Neo4J deep dive later
```

---

## Prime Directive

Build the smallest useful version of `wakil` that advances the local knowledge-work use case.

Before adding abstraction, ask:

```question
Does this clearly improve local Markdown knowledge work for one user?
```

If the answer is not obviously yes, do not add it.

Prefer simple, explicit, boring Python code over clever frameworks or speculative architecture.

---

## Design Biases

Prefer:

```text
simple local workflows
Markdown as source of truth
SQLite as operational store
QMD as first-class search
git-native changes
clear memory lifecycle
human review
rich CLI output
grounded citations
explicit commands
small composable services
```

Avoid:

```text
remote runtimes
complex permissions
large agent frameworks
hidden background behavior
automatic rewriting without review
multi-agent orchestration
premature graph databases
opaque memory systems
overly abstract plugin architectures
hosted product assumptions
```

---

## Working Agreement for Agents

When contributing to this repo:

1. Keep changes small.
2. Do not add speculative abstractions.
3. Preserve the local-first CLI focus.
4. Prefer Markdown, SQLite, QMD, and Git over new infrastructure.
5. Avoid building for multi-user or hosted deployment yet.
6. Keep model behavior behind deterministic application controls.
7. Add tests for meaningful behavior.
8. Update docs when behavior changes.
9. Respect the distinction between raw sources, durable notes, and memory.
10. Treat sensitive content carefully.
11. Show reviewable diffs for knowledge-base modifications — a pre-write
    preview for direct CLI/tool use, or the resulting pull request for an
    agent following the `mcp-coordinator` skill over MCP (docs/adr/0019).
    Both satisfy this item; it does not mean every write must block on a
    human immediately before it happens, in every context.
12. Do not silently rewrite user knowledge.

The project should feel like a careful local knowledge assistant, not a sprawling agent platform.

name: Release

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      bump:
        description: Version part to bump
        type: choice
        options:
          - patch
          - minor
          - major
        default: patch
        required: true
      dry_run:
        description: Build and preview without tagging, pushing, or publishing
        type: boolean
        default: false

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  type-check:
    name: Type check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v8.3.2
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: uv sync --locked

      - name: Type check (ty)
        run: uvx ty check .

  lint:
    name: Lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v8.3.2
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: uv sync --locked

      - name: Lint (ruff)
        run: uv run ruff check .

  test:
    name: Test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v8.3.2
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: uv sync --locked

      - name: Test (pytest)
        run: uv run pytest -q
        env:
          NO_COLOR: "1"

  version:
    name: Compute version & changelog
    needs: [type-check, lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      new_version: ${{ steps.compute.outputs.new_version }}
      new_tag: ${{ steps.compute.outputs.new_tag }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v8.3.2
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Compute next version
        id: compute
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          latest_tag="$(git describe --tags --abbrev=0 --match 'v*' 2>/dev/null || echo v0.0.0)"
          version="${latest_tag#v}"
          IFS='.' read -r major minor patch <<< "$version"

          case "${{ inputs.bump }}" in
            major)
              major=$((major + 1)); minor=0; patch=0
              ;;
            minor)
              minor=$((minor + 1)); patch=0
              ;;
            patch)
              patch=$((patch + 1))
              ;;
            *)
              echo "::error::unknown bump input: ${{ inputs.bump }}"
              exit 1
              ;;
          esac

          new_version="${major}.${minor}.${patch}"
          new_tag="v${new_version}"

          echo "Latest tag: ${latest_tag}"
          echo "New version: ${new_version} (${new_tag})"

          echo "new_version=${new_version}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "new_tag=${new_tag}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Generate changelog
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          uvx git-cliff --config cliff.toml --tag "${{ steps.compute.outputs.new_tag }}" -o CHANGELOG.md
          uvx git-cliff --config cliff.toml --tag "${{ steps.compute.outputs.new_tag }}" --unreleased --strip all > release-notes.md

      - name: Upload changelog artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: release-changelog
          path: |
            CHANGELOG.md
            release-notes.md
          if-no-files-found: error

  build:
    name: Tag, build & verify
    needs: version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    env:
      NEW_VERSION: ${{ needs.version.outputs.new_version }}
      NEW_TAG: ${{ needs.version.outputs.new_tag }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      # Must run after checkout: actions/checkout cleans the workspace
      # before checking out, which would otherwise delete these files.
      - name: Download changelog artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: release-changelog

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v8.3.2
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Commit changelog and tag release
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add CHANGELOG.md
          git commit -m "📝 docs(changelog): ${NEW_TAG}"
          git tag -a "$NEW_TAG" -m "$NEW_TAG"
          git push origin HEAD:main
          git push origin "$NEW_TAG"

      # Runs after tagging (when not a dry run) so hatch-vcs derives the
      # real, tag-matching version rather than a distance-based dev version.
      - name: Build distribution
        run: uv build

      - name: Verify built wheel version
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if ! ls dist/*"${NEW_VERSION}"*.whl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "::error::no wheel in dist/ matches expected version ${NEW_VERSION}; found: $(ls dist/ 2>/dev/null || echo '(dist/ empty)')"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "Confirmed wheel matches version ${NEW_VERSION}:"
          ls dist/*"${NEW_VERSION}"*.whl

      - name: Upload dist artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: release-dist
          path: |
            dist/*
            release-notes.md
          if-no-files-found: error

  publish:
    name: Publish
    needs: [version, build]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    env:
      NEW_TAG: ${{ needs.version.outputs.new_tag }}
    steps:
      - name: Download dist artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: release-dist

      - name: Upload dry-run preview
        if: ${{ inputs.dry_run }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: release-dry-run-${{ github.run_id }}
          path: |
            dist/*
            release-notes.md
          if-no-files-found: error

      - name: Create GitHub release
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          gh release create "$NEW_TAG" dist/* --repo "${{ github.repository }}" \
            --title "$NEW_TAG" --notes-file release-notes.md

# git-cliff configuration for wakil
# https://git-cliff.org/docs/configuration
#
# Commit convention: gitmoji-prefixed Conventional Commits, e.g.
#   "✨ feat(ingest): synthesize real content on entity create"
# `conventional_commits = false` because the leading emoji makes the raw
# messages not strictly conventional; commit_parsers below match on the
# `type(scope)?:` part after the emoji instead.

[changelog]
# A Tera template to be rendered for each release in the changelog.
# See https://keats.github.io/tera/docs/#introduction
header = """
# Changelog

All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.
"""
body = """
{% if version %}\
    ## [{{ version | trim_start_matches(pat="v") }}] - {{ timestamp | date(format="%Y-%m-%d") }}
{% else %}\
    ## [Unreleased]
{% endif %}\
{% for group, commits in commits | group_by(attribute="group") %}
    ### {{ group | striptags | trim | upper_first }}
    {% for commit in commits -%}
        - {% if commit.scope %}*({{ commit.scope }})* {% endif %}\
            {% if commit.breaking %}[**breaking**] {% endif %}\
            {{ commit.message | split(pat="\n") | first | trim | upper_first }}
    {% endfor %}
{% endfor %}
"""
footer = ""
# Remove leading and trailing whitespaces from the changelog's body.
trim = true
# Render body even when there are no releases to process.
render_always = false
# An array of regex based postprocessors to modify the changelog.
# GitHub's release-page renderer treats any bare `@word` as a user mention
# and lists matches in a "Contributors" widget -- even ones that don't name
# a real account (e.g. a commit describing wakil's own `@file:`/`@url:`
# context-reference syntax produced two bogus contributor avatars on the
# v0.1.0 release). Wrap any `@word` in backticks so it renders as code
# instead of being mention-parsed; this is a single-user project, so there's
# no real contributor mention this could ever suppress.
postprocessors = [
    { pattern = '@([A-Za-z0-9_-]+)', replace = "`@${1}`" },
]

[git]
# The project's commits are gitmoji-prefixed Conventional Commits
# (e.g. "✨ feat(ingest): ..."), not bare Conventional Commits, so the
# built-in conventional-commit parser is disabled in favor of the
# emoji-tolerant regexes in `commit_parsers` below.
conventional_commits = false
# Do not filter on conventional-commit shape; grouping/skipping is handled
# entirely by commit_parsers.
filter_unconventional = false
require_conventional = false
split_commits = false
commit_preprocessors = []
protect_breaking_commits = false

# Regexes are tolerant of a leading emoji (`^.{0,3}`, i.e. up to a couple of
# UTF-16-ish code points for the emoji + variation selector + space) before
# the `type(scope)?:` token. Order matters: skip rules must come before the
# catch-all, and specific skips (merge commits, chore/build/ci/test/style)
# come first so they never fall through into a feature/fix group.
commit_parsers = [
    { message = "^Merge pull request", skip = true },
    { message = "^.{0,3}feat(\\(.+\\))?!?:", group = "✨ Features" },
    { message = "^.{0,3}fix(\\(.+\\))?!?:", group = "🐛 Bug Fixes" },
    { message = "^.{0,3}perf(\\(.+\\))?!?:", group = "⚡ Performance" },
    { message = "^.{0,3}refactor(\\(.+\\))?!?:", group = "♻️ Refactoring" },
    { message = "^.{0,3}docs(\\(.+\\))?!?:", group = "📝 Documentation" },
    { message = "^.{0,3}chore(\\(.+\\))?!?:", skip = true },
    { message = "^.{0,3}build(\\(.+\\))?!?:", skip = true },
    { message = "^.{0,3}ci(\\(.+\\))?!?:", skip = true },
    { message = "^.{0,3}test(\\(.+\\))?!?:", skip = true },
    { message = "^.{0,3}style(\\(.+\\))?!?:", skip = true },

=== c7fca92 ===
Add an MCP interface, with a fast-capture coordinator skill (#103)

* ✨ feat(mcp): add wakil mcp serve — MCP server with read/write tools

Exposes wakil over MCP (stdio), bound to one workspace per process via the
existing -w/--workspace resolution. Read tools (status, search, query,
memory, relationships, sources, git, skills) are thin wrappers over the
existing app/*_service.py functions. Write tools are prepare/apply pairs
(ingest_prepare/apply, enrich_prepare/apply) mirroring cli/main.py's
_run_ingest/enrich sequence exactly — every write still lands on a branch
and a draft-then-ready PR, and nothing is written until a separate *_apply
call, preserving the same review checkpoint the CLI has today. A new
mcp/proposals.py in-process cache bridges prepare/apply since MCP calls,
unlike the CLI's single-process confirm flow, can happen in separate turns.

See docs/adr/0018-mcp-interface.md for the full design.

* ✨ feat(skills): add mcp-coordinator fast-capture skill

An outer-agent skill (Claude Skill format, read by the MCP client — not
one of the DAG-internal skills under src/wakil/skills/) that chains
ingest_prepare/apply and enrich_prepare/apply for low-friction capture,
pausing for a human only on genuine ambiguity (a plausible entity-
duplicate, a low-confidence/peripheral flag, a validation issue). Served
live by wakil mcp serve as the wakil://skill/mcp-coordinator MCP resource.

The policy for when to pause lives entirely in this skill's prose, not in
wakil's code — mcp/tools.py's prepare/apply split behaves identically
either way. See docs/adr/0019-fast-capture-review-tempo.md for why the
resulting pull request is an acceptable substitute for a pre-write pause
in this flow, not a bypass of one.

* 📝 docs: document wakil mcp serve and the fast-capture review tempo

README: usage section for wakil mcp serve, an example Claude Desktop
config, and a pointer to the mcp-coordinator skill.

PROMPT.md: the MCP interface as the first realization of 'additional
interfaces later,' plus the busy-operator persona this session surfaced —
a user who needs capture's interruption cost to stay low across a
high-meeting-volume day.

CLAUDE.md: clarify Working Agreement item 11 — a pre-write preview or the
resulting pull request both satisfy 'show reviewable diffs,' depending on
whether an agent is following the fast-capture skill.

TODO.md: track what's implemented and what's deliberately deferred
(memory lifecycle transition tools) for the MCP interface.

* 🐛 fix(mcp): satisfy ty — Literal direction type, None-check on Source

relationships()'s direction param was typed str while graph_service.traverse()
expects Literal["out", "in", "both"] (Direction); narrow it to match in both
mcp/tools.py and the server.py tool wrapper, which also tightens the MCP
tool's client-facing schema to the actual 3-value enum.

test_mcp_tools.py: session.get() returns Source | None; assert not-None
before reading .status.

* ✏️ chore(skills): make mcp-coordinator Hermes-ready — exact tool names, tighter description

Hermes registers MCP tools as mcp_<server_name>_<tool_name>, not the bare
names wakil's server defines — the skill now calls out that mapping and
uses the exact mcp_wakil_* names Hermes will actually show the model,
closing the name-inference gap discussed when wiring this skill up for
Hermes Agent (nousresearch/hermes-agent).

Also tightens the frontmatter description to ~55 chars, phrased as a
trigger ('Ingest a transcript, article, or note into the wakil KB')
rather than a description of the mechanism — Hermes surfaces name+
description in a token-limited skill index the model uses to judge
relevance from natural conversation, so this is the string that decides
whether the skill gets considered at all outside an explicit /mcp-coordinator
invocation.

---------

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>

=== 5170fe4 ===
Make mcp-coordinator work with multiple wakil MCP servers (#104)

* ✏️ fix(skills): make mcp-coordinator work with multiple wakil MCP servers

The skill previously hardcoded mcp_wakil_* tool names, assuming exactly
one connected wakil server. Now that a user can wire up one wakil MCP
server per knowledge base (e.g. wakil_personal, wakil_kb in Hermes's
mcp_servers config), that assumption breaks — the actual tool prefix
varies per server, and calling the wrong one would operate on the wrong
KB entirely.

The skill now instructs the agent to identify which connected server
matches the knowledge base the user means before calling anything, ask
if it's ambiguous, and never mix servers within one source's
capture+enrich sequence. Tool references in the flow body are back to
their bare wakil names (ingest_prepare, etc.) with the prefix resolution
explained once up front, rather than repeating one hardcoded prefix
throughout.

* 📝 docs(troubleshooting): record the uv run --env-file gotcha

Discovered wiring wakil mcp serve into Hermes's mcp_servers config: uv
run does not auto-load a project's .env, contrary to what seemed like a
reasonable assumption (and what the existing CLI-shelling Hermes skill's
guidance implicitly relied on). Confirmed empirically with a stripped
environment, both with and without --env-file.

---------

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>

=== f878628 ===
Pin mcp SDK below v2 to fix ModuleNotFoundError on wakil mcp serve (#105)

* 🐛 fix(deps): pin mcp SDK below v2 — 2.0.0 breaks mcp.server.fastmcp

mcp>=1.2 had no upper bound. A fresh resolve (uv tool install, which
does its own resolution rather than using this repo's uv.lock) picked
up mcp 2.0.0, a breaking major release that restructures
mcp.server.fastmcp to mcp.server.mcpserver — ModuleNotFoundError on
'wakil mcp serve' every time, since src/wakil/mcp/server.py imports
FastMCP from the old path.

Pinned to mcp>=1.2,<2, matching the API surface the code actually
targets; re-locked (still resolves to 1.28.1) and re-verified the
import, full test suite, ruff, and ty all pass.

* 📝 docs(troubleshooting): record the uv tool install vs uv.lock mcp 2.0.0 break

Explains why 'wakil mcp serve' failed with ModuleNotFoundError on a
uv tool install-managed ~/.local/bin/wakil while uv run --project (this
session's own invocation path, and CI) kept working the whole time —
the tool install does its own fresh dependency resolution rather than
consulting the repo's committed uv.lock.

---------

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>

=== 46aea3a ===
✨ feat(cli): add --version flag alongside the version subcommand (#107)

Standard eager-callback pattern: wakil --version prints and exits
before workspace resolution runs, so it works from any directory with
no -w needed, same as wakil version already did.

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>

=== 14ddb0a ===
✏️ chore(skills): note enrich_prepare/apply are slow, hint at non-blocking calls (#106)

enrich runs two real LLM calls (extraction, entity resolution) and can
take several minutes on a long source — a real timeout was hit against
Hermes before its per-server MCP timeout was raised. Investigated
whether wakil could suggest an MCP-level 'background' mode for this
specific tool call: Hermes's own docs show background=true/process()
polling is scoped to the terminal tool only, with no documented
backgrounding for MCP tool calls generally. Separately, observed that
Claude's own agent loop handles a long MCP tool call fine once hinted
it'll be slow — this is client agent-loop behavior, not something the
MCP protocol or wakil's server needs to expose.

So the skill now just tells the agent to warn the user up front and use
whatever non-blocking-call mechanism its own harness offers, if any —
generic guidance that works whether or not the specific client has an
explicit backgrounding feature, rather than assuming one client's
mechanism (e.g. Hermes's terminal-only background=true) applies
everywhere.

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>

Pinned to mcp>=1.2,<2, matching the API surface the code actually
targets; re-locked (still resolves to 1.28.1) and re-verified the
import, full test suite, ruff, and ty all pass.

* 📝 docs(troubleshooting): record the uv tool install vs uv.lock mcp 2.0.0 break

Explains why 'wakil mcp serve' failed with ModuleNotFoundError on a
uv tool install-managed ~/.local/bin/wakil while uv run --project (this
session's own invocation path, and CI) kept working the whole time —
the tool install does its own fresh dependency resolution rather than
consulting the repo's committed uv.lock.

---------

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>

=== 46aea3a ===
✨ feat(cli): add --version flag alongside the version subcommand (#107)

Standard eager-callback pattern: wakil --version prints and exits
before workspace resolution runs, so it works from any directory with
no -w needed, same as wakil version already did.

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>

=== 14ddb0a ===
✏️ chore(skills): note enrich_prepare/apply are slow, hint at non-blocking calls (#106)

enrich runs two real LLM calls (extraction, entity resolution) and can
take several minutes on a long source — a real timeout was hit against
Hermes before its per-server MCP timeout was raised. Investigated
whether wakil could suggest an MCP-level 'background' mode for this
specific tool call: Hermes's own docs show background=true/process()
polling is scoped to the terminal tool only, with no documented
backgrounding for MCP tool calls generally. Separately, observed that
Claude's own agent loop handles a long MCP tool call fine once hinted
it'll be slow — this is client agent-loop behavior, not something the
MCP protocol or wakil's server needs to expose.

So the skill now just tells the agent to warn the user up front and use
whatever non-blocking-call mechanism its own harness offers, if any —
generic guidance that works whether or not the specific client has an
explicit backgrounding feature, rather than assuming one client's
mechanism (e.g. Hermes's terminal-only background=true) applies
everywhere.

Co-authored-by: test <test@test.com>
